title: Year three close
hook: the long story is told; next year, the ways of the Guru: ragas, teachings, and the living panth

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at renewal and today; your line was everywhere, still rising. Today is the last day of year three.

A storyteller's Nanak. A weaver's songs in the Guru's book. A servant sent north. Families shielded in a moving ring. A gold roof, a boy far from home, protesters who didn't strike back, a kitchen that feeds whoever comes. That's this year in one breath, from day six hundred ninety-seven, when Bhai Gurdas opened it, to this one. Each picture is a name that became a story.
screen: `A STORYTELLER, A WEAVER, A SERVANT.` → `A YEAR IN ONE BREATH.` → `NAMES THAT BECAME STORIES.`

segments.voice: Look at the shape of it. Year one gave you the path's words, stories, practices and the Japji. Year two gave you the daily banis, a day lived in the Guru's words. Year three gave you a people's memory. It began with the tellers: Bhai Gurdas, Bhai Nand Lal, the janamsakhis, and the Bhagats. Then the people around the Gurus. Then the hard century, the misls, the kingdom and its loss. Then reform, the twentieth century, and the calendar of days on which Sikhs remember. Why a whole year on history? Listen to the Ardas. Before it asks for anything, it remembers: the Gurus by name, the four Sahibzade, the five beloved ones, the forty liberated ones, and the martyrs who kept their faith. Every time a Sikh stands for the Ardas, the long story is told again in a few minutes. So the history isn't a school subject sitting beside the faith. It's inside the prayer. Whoever stands for the Ardas stands among everyone it names: the story holds us. Now turn and face the other way. Year four is the ways of the Guru: the ragas the Granth is set in, the teachings opened slowly, and the living panth, the community as it lives now. Tomorrow begins with a question about sound, and why the Gurus' words were meant to be sung. This year's faces won't vanish. Bhai Gurdas's vars, for one, are sung in kirtan beside the Guru's words.
screen: `THREE YEARS: WORDS, A DAY, A MEMORY.` · `THE ARDAS TELLS THE STORY AGAIN.` · `HISTORY INSIDE THE PRAYER.` · `YEAR FOUR: THE WAYS OF THE GURU.` · then, large: `THE STORY HOLDS US.`

segments.voice: Lean back, let the shoulders drop, and for a while do nothing at all while the year settles: the tellers, the martyrs, the kings, the exiles, the kitchens. Toward the end, look forward to a sound: a harmonium, a voice, a line of the Guru's words set to music. If you pray, say Waheguru once, as thanks for the year; if you don't, simply let tomorrow have some room in it.
Ardas. The standing prayer that remembers the long story, the tellers, the saints, the hard century, the kingdom and its loss, renewal and today, before it asks for anything. Today's word.
Your line: the story holds us. Three years walked, and the hill keeps going. Year three, done.

howItsDone: In the Ardas, said standing at the end of Sikh prayers and gatherings, Sikhs remember the Gurus, the Sahibzade, the Panj Pyare, the forty liberated ones and the martyrs before making their requests, so the community's history is recalled every time it is said.

chat.says: Why would a prayer spend so long listing names from history?
options: In the Ardas, remembering comes first, so the story is told again every time it's said.
It's a way to show off a long history before getting to the real prayer at the end.
It doesn't; the Ardas only asks for things, and history is kept out of it.
chat.meaning: Before it asks for anything, the Ardas remembers the Gurus, the Sahibzade and the martyrs, so the history lives inside the prayer.

Ardas.meaning: the standing prayer that remembers before it asks

Sahibzade.meaning: the four sons of Guru Gobind Singh

Japji.meaning: Guru Nanak's hymn at the start of the Guru Granth Sahib

banis.meaning: the daily prayers drawn from the Guru's words

panth.meaning: the Sikh community, the path as a people
